title: Darjeeling Tea Gardens: Flushes, Visits and Buying
meta_description: Visit Darjeeling's tea gardens: the 1841 story, first to autumn flush, Happy Valley, Lopchu and Peshok, how tea is made and how to buy without being fleeced.
summary: Darjeeling has about 87 tea gardens, and you can walk to one, Happy Valley, from the town centre. Visit between March and November, when plucking is on and factories work. First flush (March–April) is light and floral, second flush (May–June) fuller and muscatel. Buy from a garden or a shop that names the estate, flush and year.

sections.heading: How a doctor's garden became Darjeeling tea
paras: Tea in Darjeeling began as an experiment in a garden. Dr Archibald Campbell, an Indian Medical Service officer who became superintendent of the young hill station in 1839, planted China tea seeds at his house, Beechwood, around 1841. The bushes grew well in the cool, wet air at about 2,000 m, and others followed his lead. By 1852 the first commercial gardens were being laid out, among them Tukvar, Steinthal and Aloobari, on slopes that had been forest a few years earlier.

The gardens needed labour, and most of the workers who cleared the slopes and plucked the leaf came from eastern Nepal. Their descendants still make up most of the workforce, and the Nepali language, food and festivals of Darjeeling grew out of the tea estates as much as the town. Today there are about 87 gardens in the Darjeeling hills. In 2004 Darjeeling tea became India's first product to carry a Geographical Indication, which means only tea grown and made in those gardens may be sold under the name.

sections.heading: The four flushes, and how they taste
paras: A flush is a season of new growth. The bushes rest through the cold, dry winter, and plucking stops roughly from December to February. When the growth returns, each season gives a different tea, and the names on the packets refer to these seasons. Prices follow taste and demand: the best first flush teas from famous gardens fetch high prices at auction, while monsoon tea is the everyday cup.

sections.heading: Visiting Happy Valley from town
paras: Happy Valley Tea Estate, one of the older gardens of the district, lies on Lebong Cart Road just below the town, roughly a half-hour walk downhill from Chowrasta or a short taxi ride. It is the easiest garden to visit without a car, and the walk down through the bushes, with pickers working the rows in season, is reason enough to go.

In the plucking season the factory usually lets visitors see part of the process, sometimes for a small fee, and there is a tasting and sales room. Visiting hours vary, the factory is quiet when there is no leaf to process, and it may be closed on some days, so check current status before you travel. Mornings are best, when the morning's leaf is coming in. Walk back up slowly: the climb to the Mall is steep.

sections.heading: Gardens on the Peshok and Takdah side
paras: The road from Ghoom down through Jorebunglow to Lopchu, Peshok and Teesta Bazar runs through some of the best-known tea of the district. Lopchu estate is a familiar name on Indian shelves, and the small tea shops on the roadside around Lopchu sell packets and cups to passing travellers. Lower down, the Peshok estate covers steep slopes above the Teesta valley, with the view point over the meeting of the Teesta and Rangeet a short drive on. Most travellers pass this way on the road to Kalimpong or Gangtok, and a tea stop costs only half an hour.

Turn off toward Takdah and Tinchuley and you reach Rungli Rungliot and Gielle. The local story is that Rungli Rungliot means "thus far and no further"; we have not seen a written source for how the name arose, so treat it as folklore. Many homestays in Tinchuley and Takdah are run by families who work in these gardens, and a host may walk you through the rows and explain the plucking. Further out, Mim estate near Jorepokhri and Ging on the way down to Bijanbari show how wide the tea country spreads.

sections.heading: From leaf to cup: what you will see
paras: Darjeeling tea is mostly orthodox tea, made by a method that keeps the leaf whole rather than crushing it into small grains. A factory visit follows the leaf through five steps, and knowing them makes the noise and smell of the factory floor make sense.
list: Plucking: pickers, most of them women, take two leaves and a bud by hand and carry them in baskets on their backs to the weighing point.
Withering: the leaf is spread in long troughs and air is blown through it for many hours until it loses much of its water and turns soft.
Rolling: machines twist and bruise the leaf, breaking its cells so the juices meet the air.
Oxidation: the rolled leaf rests and darkens; the tea maker decides by smell and colour when to stop it, and this step shapes the taste most.
Drying and sorting: hot air dries the leaf, then it is sieved into grades, with whole leaf at the top and broken leaf, fannings and dust below.

sections.heading: Planning a tea day, and garden manners
paras: The cheapest tea day costs almost nothing: walk down to Happy Valley in the morning, then come back to town for a pot in one of the tea rooms around the Mall, where a cup or pot of Darjeeling costs about ₹40–150. For a fuller day, hire a car for about ₹2,500–4,000 and drive the Peshok road, stopping at the roadside tea shops near Lopchu and the Teesta view point, and returning by Lamahatta. Better still, spend a night in a Takdah or Tinchuley homestay and walk through the gardens at plucking time with your host.

Remember that a tea estate is a workplace and a village, not a park. Stay on the paths between the rows, do not pick leaves, and ask before photographing the pickers, many of whom are happy to chat if you greet them first. Walking among the bushes in a garden's private section may need permission from the office, and factory floors have their own safety rules. Wear shoes with grip, since the paths are steep and slippery after rain.

sections.heading: Buying tea without being fleeced
paras: Darjeeling sells far more tea labelled Darjeeling than the gardens could ever grow, and the town's shops range from honest family businesses to stalls selling ordinary blends in fancy boxes. The good news is that a few simple checks protect you.

Buy loose leaf you can see and smell, not tea bags or dust in gift tins. Ask which garden the tea came from, which flush and which year; a good seller will tell you straight away, and many packets print it. Look for the Tea Board's Darjeeling logo on branded packs. Ask to taste before you buy a large amount, and compare two or three teas side by side: the difference between a first and second flush is easy to taste. Buying at a garden's own sales room, as at Happy Valley, removes most of the doubt.

Prices vary enormously. As a rough indicative guide for 2025–26, everyday Darjeeling sells for a few hundred rupees per 100 g, while good first and second flush teas from named gardens can cost ₹500 to well over ₹1,500 per 100 g. Anything selling as top garden first flush for very little money is probably not what it claims. Buy small amounts of several teas rather than a kilo of one, and store them airtight and away from light.

faqs.q: Can I visit a tea garden in Darjeeling without a car?
faqs.a: Yes. Happy Valley Tea Estate is on Lebong Cart Road just below the town, roughly a half-hour walk downhill from Chowrasta. You can walk through the bushes and, in the plucking season, usually see part of the factory and taste tea. Visiting hours and fees change, and the factory may close on some days, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Darjeeling tea gardens?
faqs.a: March to November, when the bushes are being plucked and the factories are working. April brings the first flush and fresh green slopes; May and June the second flush; October and November the autumn flush with clearer mountain views. From December to February the bushes rest, plucking stops and factories are mostly quiet, though the gardens are still pleasant to walk through.

faqs.q: What is the difference between first flush and second flush Darjeeling tea?
faqs.a: First flush is plucked in March and April after the winter rest and is light, floral and slightly green, with a pale golden cup. Second flush comes in May and June and is fuller and rounder, with the muscatel note Darjeeling is famous for and an amber colour. First flush suits drinking plain; second flush stands up to a little milk.

faqs.q: When did tea growing start in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Dr Archibald Campbell, the superintendent of Darjeeling from 1839, planted China tea seeds in his garden at Beechwood around 1841. The plants did well, and from 1852 the first commercial gardens, including Tukvar, Steinthal and Aloobari, were established. The industry grew fast with workers from eastern Nepal, and today there are about 87 gardens in the hills.

faqs.q: What does the Darjeeling tea GI tag mean?
faqs.a: In 2004 Darjeeling tea became India's first product with a Geographical Indication. It means that only tea grown and processed in the registered gardens of the Darjeeling hills may legally be sold as Darjeeling tea. When buying, look for the Tea Board's Darjeeling logo on branded packs and ask for the garden name, which genuine sellers give readily.

faqs.q: How much does good Darjeeling tea cost?
faqs.a: As an indicative 2025–26 guide, everyday Darjeeling sells for a few hundred rupees per 100 g, and good first or second flush from a named garden can cost ₹500 to well over ₹1,500 per 100 g. Auction teas from famous estates cost far more. Be wary of very cheap tea sold as top garden first flush, and taste before buying in quantity.

faqs.q: Which tea gardens can I see on the way to Kalimpong or Gangtok?
faqs.a: The road from Ghoom down through Jorebunglow to Teesta Bazar passes Lopchu and Peshok estates, with roadside tea shops near Lopchu where you can taste and buy. A short detour leads to the Teesta and Rangeet confluence viewpoint above Peshok. Roads on the Teesta side are sometimes closed after landslides, so check current status before you travel.

The local story is that Rungli Rungliot, a tea estate near Takdah and Tinchuley, means "thus far and no further". We treat this as folklore, since we have not seen the name's origin in a written record. The estate is easy to see on a Takdah and Tinchuley homestay trip, where many hosts work in nearby gardens.

faqs.q: How should I brew Darjeeling tea?
faqs.a: Use about one teaspoon (2–3 g) of loose leaf per cup, water just off the boil, and steep for 3–4 minutes; first flush often tastes better at the shorter end. Try it plain first, since milk and sugar hide the flavour, especially of first flush. Keep the leaf in an airtight tin away from light and strong smells, and finish it within a year.
